Complaint: A 3-month history of progressively worsening stiffness and deep, aching pain in the left shoulder, worse at night, with difficulty reaching behind the back, combing hair, and fastening a bra. No preceding trauma.
Analysis: The clinical picture is classic for adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder). The strongest supporting facts are the global restriction of both active and passive range of motion of the left shoulder, particularly the marked limitation of external rotation (20 degrees vs. 70 degrees on the right), in a patient with a 10-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus—a well-established risk factor. The absence of focal tenderness over rotator cuff tendons, the lack of trauma, and unremarkable radiographs (no fracture, dislocation, or advanced osteoarthritis) further support this diagnosis. Main differential considerations include rotator cuff tear, glenohumeral osteoarthritis, calcific tendinitis, cervical radiculopathy, and less likely septic arthritis or malignancy. The global restriction of passive motion and lack of focal tenderness favor adhesive capsulitis over most of these. No red flags (fever, acute trauma, neurovascular compromise, systemic symptoms) are present.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None further required initially; the diagnosis is clinical and radiographs are already available. If conservative management fails or diagnostic uncertainty arises, shoulder ultrasound or MRI may be obtained to assess rotator cuff integrity and rule out intra-articular pathology. Baseline inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) are not routinely needed unless infection or inflammatory arthritis is suspected.
Conclusion: Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) of the left shoulder, likely secondary to long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus. The condition is non-emergent and best managed by an orthopedic specialist with conservative therapy.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics

winner_protocol:
Age: 40 years

Sex: Male

Complaint: A 10-day history of worsening facial pressure, purulent nasal discharge, nasal congestion, and anosmia in a patient with known chronic rhinosinusitis and bilateral nasal polyps, accompanied by postnasal drip and a productive cough worse at night.

Analysis: The patient has a known history of chronic rhinosinusitis with bilateral nasal polyps, recurrent sinus infections (4–5 per year), and prior polypectomy two years ago. The current 10-day worsening of purulent nasal discharge, facial pressure, congestion, and anosmia, together with exam findings of edematous and erythematous nasal mucosa, visible polypoid tissue, mucopurulent drainage in the middle meatus, and tenderness over the maxillary and frontal sinuses, is most consistent with an acute bacterial exacerbation superimposed on chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP). The absence of fever, visual changes, and severe headache, and the lack of orbital or intracranial signs on exam, indicate a non-emergent presentation. Main differential considerations include allergic fungal rhinosinusitis, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD/Samter's triad), mucocele, odontogenic sinusitis, eosinophilic CRS, and—per one expert—nasopharyngeal carcinoma, particularly given the recurrent and refractory nature of the disease. The oropharyngeal cobblestoning suggests possible lower airway involvement or postnasal drip-related irritation.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Nasal endoscopy to confirm findings, assess polyp burden, and obtain culture of purulent drainage; non-contrast CT of the paranasal sinuses if not recently performed or if complications, anatomic obstruction, or surgical planning are being considered; allergy testing and/or aspirin challenge if AERD is suspected; evaluation for eosinophilia or allergic/fungal contributors.

Conclusion: This is an acute bacterial exacerbation of chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) in a patient with recurrent, refractory disease. There are no red flags for orbital or intracranial complications, and the condition can be managed on a non-emergent outpatient basis under the care of an otolaryngologist.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)

Recommendations: Initiate empiric antibiotic therapy (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate) for the acute bacterial exacerbation, ideally guided by endoscopic culture. Add intranasal corticosteroid spray and saline nasal irrigation as foundational therapy for CRSwNP. Consider a short course of systemic corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone 20–30 mg daily for 5–7 days) if significant polyp edema is present. Arrange timely ENT follow-up for endoscopic evaluation and possible surgical planning. Screen for aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD), given the strong association with refractory CRSwNP. Consider allergic fungal rhinosinusitis, especially if eosinophilia, characteristic CT findings, or fungal elements are present. Evaluate for underlying immunodeficiencies (e.g., IgG subclass deficiency) given more than four sinus infections per year. Assess for comorbid asthma or eosinophilic bronchitis, as postnasal drip and cobblestoning may indicate lower airway involvement. Verify medication adherence and proper intranasal corticosteroid technique, as inadequate delivery to polypoid tissue is a common cause of treatment failure. Consider baseline olfactory testing to monitor anosmia, which may reflect polyp burden and impact quality of life. If medical therapy fails after 4–6 weeks, obtain CT sinus imaging to assess for anatomic obstruction or mucocele formation, and discuss escalation to revision endoscopic sinus surgery or biologic therapy (e.g., dupilumab) for refractory disease. Review prior antibiotic courses and recent microbiology results to guide antibiotic selection. Inquire about smoking status, occupational exposures, and allergen sensitization. Assess for sleep-disordered breathing given nocturnal cough and nasal obstruction, and review vaccination status (influenza, COVID-19) as it may affect risk of secondary infections.

Notes: The patient denies fever, visual changes, and severe headache; these red flags—along with periorbital edema or erythema, frontal swelling, meningeal signs, and neurological deficits—must be actively sought during evaluation, as their presence would indicate orbital or intracranial extension requiring emergent imaging and intervention. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma was raised as a differential by one expert and may warrant consideration in persistent or unilateral disease. Biologic therapy is not standard initial management but may be considered for refractory cases.

Age: 35  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Progressive bilateral submandibular and sublingual swelling with worsening trismus, odynophagia, muffled "hot potato" voice, drooling, and respiratory distress, occurring 5 days after extraction of the lower left second molar.  
Analysis: The clinical picture is most consistent with Ludwig's angina—a rapidly progressive, bilateral deep neck space infection involving the submandibular and sublingual spaces. Strong supporting facts include the antecedent lower left second molar extraction (whose roots extend below the mylohyoid line, a classic portal for spread into the submandibular space), the woody, erythematous bilateral submandibular swelling, elevation and induration of the floor of the mouth with posterior/superior tongue displacement, trismus, and the muffled voice. The patient's inspiratory stridor, drooling, SpO2 of 91% on room air, and upright posture with respiratory distress indicate critical oropharyngeal airway narrowing, corroborated by CT showing a multiloculated fluid collection in the submandibular and sublingual spaces bilaterally with significant airway compromise. Main differential considerations include other deep neck space infections (parapharyngeal abscess, retropharyngeal abscess, peritonsillar abscess), epiglottitis, angioedema, and necrotizing fasciitis of the neck; however, the bilateral submandibular/sublingual distribution and dental trigger make Ludwig's angina the most likely diagnosis.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Airway equipment for awake fiberoptic intubation and emergency surgical airway (tracheostomy set); baseline labs (CBC with differential, basic metabolic panel, CRP/ESR, blood cultures); bedside neck ultrasound to delineate fluid collections if CT is delayed; repeat neck imaging (CT) 24–48 hours post-drainage to confirm resolution if clinically indicated.  
Conclusion: This is Ludwig's angina with impending airway obstruction, requiring emergent airway control, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and prompt surgical drainage of the submandibular and sublingual spaces, followed by ICU monitoring.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)  
Recommendations: 1) Secure the airway immediately—awake fiberoptic intubation or emergency tracheostomy under local anesthesia—before any other intervention, given stridor, hypoxia, and CT-demonstrated airway narrowing; avoid supine positioning. 2) Start empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering oral flora (streptococci and anaerobes), e.g., ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin plus ceftriaxone. 3) Perform prompt surgical drainage (incision and drainage, transcervical or intraoral) of the submandibular and sublingual fluid collections for source control. 4) Admit to the intensive care unit (ICU) for continuous airway monitoring, sepsis management, IV fluid resuscitation, analgesia, and antipyretics. 5) Obtain blood cultures and baseline labs to guide therapy and assess systemic response. 6) Arrange dental evaluation for definitive source control of the extracted tooth site. 7) Plan serial airway examinations and repeat neck imaging 24–48 hours post-drainage to ensure resolution; complete a total 10–14-day course of antibiotics (IV then oral). Multidisciplinary coordination among Emergency Medicine, Otolaryngology (ENT), and Anesthesiology is essential.  
Notes: Airway protection takes precedence over all other diagnostic or therapeutic steps; any delay risks complete airway obstruction. The patient should remain upright and monitored continuously until the airway is secured.

Vignette:
A 24-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks gestation is brought in by ambulance after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home lasting approximately 2 minutes. Her partner reports she has complained of a persistent headache, visual disturbances described as flashing lights, and swelling of her face and hands over the past 2 days. She did not attend her last two prenatal appointments. On examination, she is postictal, moaning, and not following commands. Vital signs: T 37.6C, HR 112, RR 22, BP 182/116, SpO2 94%. Significant periorbital and bilateral upper extremity edema is present. Deep tendon reflexes are 4+ bilaterally with sustained clonus at the ankles. Fetal heart rate monitoring shows persistent late decelerations. Labs: platelets 92,000/mcL, AST 286 U/L, ALT 312 U/L, LDH 680 U/L, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 5.2. IV magnesium sulfate is initiated and emergent cesarean delivery is planned.
winner_protocol:
Age: 24 years

Sex: Female

Complaint: A 24-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks gestation presents after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home lasting approximately 2 minutes, preceded by a 2-day history of persistent headache, visual disturbances (flashing lights), and facial and hand swelling. She is postictal on arrival with severe hypertension, significant edema, hyperreflexia with sustained clonus, and fetal heart rate tracing showing persistent late decelerations.

Analysis: The clinical picture is consistent with eclampsia secondary to severe preeclampsia with HELLP syndrome. Strongest supporting facts include: (1) a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure in a pregnant patient at 36 weeks; (2) severe hypertension (BP 182/116 mmHg); (3) proteinuria (urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 5.2); (4) thrombocytopenia (platelets 92,000/mcL); (5) elevated liver enzymes (AST 286 U/L, ALT 312 U/L, LDH 680 U/L) indicating hemolysis and hepatic injury; (6) renal impairment (creatinine 1.4 mg/dL); (7) hyperreflexia with sustained ankle clonus, headache, and visual disturbances reflecting CNS irritability; and (8) persistent fetal late decelerations indicating uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal distress. The condition is life-threatening for both mother and fetus, requiring immediate intervention. Main differential considerations include primary seizure disorder (epilepsy), intracranial hemorrhage, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, hypertensive encephalopathy, metabolic disturbances (e.g., hypoglycemia, electrolyte imbalance), and meningitis/encephalitis; these should be considered especially if atypical features emerge or seizures recur despite therapeutic magnesium levels.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Complete blood count (already showing thrombocytopenia), liver enzymes (AST/ALT), LDH, serum creatinine, coagulation profile (PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen), peripheral smear, uric acid, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, continuous fetal heart rate monitoring, bedside obstetric ultrasound for fetal status, continuous non-invasive blood pressure monitoring, and, after maternal stabilization, neuroimaging (CT/MRI) if intracranial pathology is suspected.

Conclusion: This is an obstetric emergency — eclampsia with severe features of preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome — complicated by fetal distress. The definitive treatment is emergent delivery of the fetus and placenta, with concurrent maternal stabilization using magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis and antihypertensive therapy to control severe hypertension.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology

Recommendations:
1. Continue IV magnesium sulfate: 4-g IV loading dose, then 1-g/hr infusion (adjust for renal function given creatinine 1.4 mg/dL), for seizure prophylaxis and prevention of recurrent seizures.
2. Control severe hypertension with rapid-acting IV antihypertensives (e.g., labetalol, hydralazine, or nicardipine) to maintain BP < 160/110 mmHg.
3. Proceed with emergent cesarean delivery without delay, given persistent fetal late decelerations and the maternal condition; coordinate with anesthesia (consider general anesthesia if coagulopathy or severe thrombocytopenia is present) and have the neonatal team ready for resuscitation.
4. Prepare for potential blood product administration (platelets or plasma) if bleeding risk is high or coagulopathy develops.
5. Continue continuous fetal monitoring until delivery.
6. Post-delivery: continue magnesium sulfate for 24 hours; monitor blood pressure, organ function, and laboratory values; watch for postpartum eclampsia, HELLP syndrome persistence or worsening, DIC, or hepatic rupture.
7. Counsel regarding postpartum antihypertensive management and future pregnancy risk.

Notes: The patient missed her last two prenatal appointments, which likely delayed recognition of preeclampsia; this highlights the importance of antenatal care. Magnesium sulfate is the standard of care for eclampsia and is superior to other anticonvulsants in this setting. Neuroimaging should be reserved for atypical neurologic signs or seizures recurring despite therapeutic magnesium levels.

A 16-year-old female volleyball player presents with mild right ankle pain after landing awkwardly on another player's foot during practice 2 hours ago. She was able to walk off the court on her own. Age: 16
Sex: Female
Complaint: Mild right ankle pain after landing awkwardly on another player's foot during volleyball practice 2 hours ago; she was able to walk off the court on her own.
Analysis: The mechanism of injury (inversion/awkward landing), localized mild tenderness over the anterior talofibular ligament, mild lateral swelling, absence of ecchymosis, ability to bear weight with minimal discomfort, and negative anterior drawer and talar tilt tests are all consistent with a Grade I (mild) lateral ankle sprain involving the ATFL. The Ottawa Ankle Rules are negative (no bony tenderness over the malleoli or foot, and ability to bear weight), so a clinically significant fracture is unlikely. No red flags are present: no severe pain, no neurovascular compromise, no deformity, no inability to bear weight, and no rapidly expanding swelling. Differential considerations include peroneal tendon injury, syndesmotic (high ankle) sprain, lateral malleolar fracture, and osteochondral lesion of the talus; however, these are less likely given the negative bony tenderness, negative stress tests, and preserved weight-bearing. The injury is mild, stable, and self-limiting.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. Plain radiographs are not currently indicated per the Ottawa Ankle Rules; imaging may be considered if swelling worsens, pain persists with weight-bearing, or if there is any doubt about fracture.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None initially. Spirometry or peak flow measurement may be considered if asthma is suspected or symptoms persist; chest X-ray is reserved for cases with fever, focal findings, hypoxia, or symptoms persisting beyond 3 weeks.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine

Age: 24
Sex: Male
Complaint: A painful small bump in the beard area that appeared 2 days after shaving with a multi-blade razor against the grain. The patient denies fever, spreading redness, or drainage. Examination reveals a single erythematous, firm papule approximately 4 mm in diameter on the right submandibular area, with mild surrounding swelling and a curled hair visible beneath the skin surface. No fluctuance, induration, or streaking erythema is present.

Analysis: The clinical presentation is consistent with pseudofolliculitis barbae (ingrown hair/razor bump). The strongest supporting facts are the temporal relationship to shaving, the use of a multi-blade razor and against-the-grain technique (both well-established risk factors for hair re-entry), the location in the beard area, and the pathognomonic finding of a curled hair visible beneath the skin surface. The absence of fever, spreading redness, drainage, fluctuance, induration, and streaking erythema rules out cellulitis, abscess formation, and systemic infection, supporting a benign, localized, self-limited process. Differential considerations include bacterial folliculitis, furuncle/abscess, epidermal inclusion cyst, acne vulgaris, herpes simplex, contact dermatitis, foreign-body granuloma, and rarely tinea barbae or cutaneous mycobacterial infection; however, the visible ingrown hair and shaving history strongly favor pseudofolliculitis barbae. No red flags are present.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None; this is a clinical diagnosis based on history and physical examination. No laboratory or imaging studies are indicated. If purulent drainage were to develop, a wound culture could be considered. If diagnostic doubt arises, dermoscopy or biopsy could be considered.

Conclusion: This is a case of pseudofolliculitis barbae (ingrown hair) presenting as a solitary, painful, erythematous papule with a visible curled hair in the beard area, precipitated by shaving against the grain with a multi-blade razor. The condition is localized, mild, and non-urgent, with no signs of secondary bacterial infection or systemic involvement. It is appropriate for self-care management with shaving modification, and dermatology is the most specific specialty for ongoing management if needed.

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations:
- Apply warm compresses to the area several times daily to reduce inflammation and help the hair surface.
- Gently extract the ingrown hair with a sterile needle or forceps once the tip is accessible; avoid digging into the skin.
- Apply a topical antiseptic (e.g., benzoyl peroxide) or a topical antibiotic (e.g., mupirocin) to prevent secondary bacterial infection.
- Advise the patient to avoid manual squeezing or picking at the lesion, as this can worsen inflammation and lead to secondary infection.
- Discontinue or modify shaving: temporarily stop shaving the affected area until resolved; avoid multi-blade razors and shaving against the grain; use a single-blade razor or electric clipper instead.
- Shave in the direction of hair growth, exfoliate the area regularly, and use a moisturizing shave gel or aftershave lotion.
- Avoid tight collars that may irritate the area.
- Monitor for red flags: fever, rapidly expanding erythema, lymphangitic streaking, fluctuance/abscess formation, severe pain, or purulent drainage. If any develop, reassess promptly; if the lesion becomes fluctuant, incision and drainage may be needed and culture should be considered.
- Consider MRSA coverage if the lesion worsens or fails to improve despite appropriate self-care.
- Assess for immunocompromising conditions (e.g., diabetes, HIV); if present, closer monitoring is warranted as even minor follicular lesions carry increased risk of progression to bacterial infection.
- For recurrent or severe cases, consider laser hair removal; recurrent lesions in the beard area might also suggest hidradenitis suppurativa and warrant further evaluation.
- If lesions worsen or become pustular despite shave modification, consider tinea barbae in the differential.
- Note that allergic or irritant contact dermatitis from shaving products can coexist and worsen inflammation; consider switching products if this is suspected.

Notes:
- Pseudofolliculitis barbae is more common and often more severe in individuals with tightly curled hair, particularly of African, Mediterranean, or South Asian descent; occupational requirements for close shaving (e.g., military, law enforcement) may complicate management.
- Recurrent or severe pseudofolliculitis can lead to scarring, keloid formation, and hyperpigmentation.

winner_protocol:
Age: 28
Sex: Female
Complaint: Sudden onset of severe left-sided pelvic pain with lightheadedness, 7 weeks of amenorrhea, and a positive home pregnancy test 5 days prior.
Analysis: The patient presents with classic features of a ruptured left tubal ectopic pregnancy with massive hemoperitoneum and hemorrhagic shock. Strong supporting facts include: 7 weeks of amenorrhea with a positive pregnancy test; quantitative beta-hCG of 4,200 mIU/mL (above the discriminatory zone where an intrauterine pregnancy should be visible); transvaginal ultrasound showing an empty uterus, a complex left adnexal mass with ring-of-fire sign, and significant free fluid in the pelvis and Morison's pouch; hemodynamic instability (BP 78/48, HR 132, pale, diaphoretic); peritoneal signs; and hemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL indicating significant blood loss. Her history of pelvic inflammatory disease and prior left tubal ectopic pregnancy treated with methotrexate are major risk factors for recurrent ectopic pregnancy. Main differential considerations include ruptured hemorrhagic ovarian cyst, corpus luteum hemorrhage, tubo-ovarian abscess from PID, ovarian torsion with infarction, acute appendicitis, and heterotopic pregnancy; however, the combination of positive hCG, empty uterus, adnexal mass with vascular flow, and hemodynamic instability strongly favors ruptured ectopic pregnancy.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Type and cross-match for blood; repeat CBC with hemoglobin; coagulation profile; assessment of Rh status. (Quantitative beta-hCG and transvaginal ultrasound have already been performed.)
Conclusion: Ruptured left tubal ectopic pregnancy with massive hemoperitoneum and decompensated hemorrhagic shock. This is an immediately life-threatening gynecologic emergency requiring emergent surgical intervention without delay to prevent exsanguination and death.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology
Recommendations: 1) Initiate rapid IV crystalloid resuscitation and blood product transfusion with O-negative packed red blood cells; activate massive transfusion protocol if needed. 2) Proceed immediately to emergent laparotomy (or laparoscopy only if hemodynamics improve) with left salpingectomy or cornual resection as indicated. 3) Administer Rh immunoglobulin if the patient is Rh-negative. 4) Give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone plus metronidazole) given the history of PID and possible tubo-ovarian abscess. 5) Post-operatively, monitor vital signs, urine output, and serial beta-hCG until nondetectable to ensure complete resolution and exclude persistent trophoblastic tissue. 6) Provide counseling on future fertility, the high risk of recurrent ectopic pregnancy, contraception options, and evaluation for tubal disease (e.g., hysterosalpingography) if desired, along with psychological support. Methotrexate is not appropriate in this case because the ectopic is ruptured and the patient is hemodynamically unstable.
Notes: Methotrexate is contraindicated in ruptured ectopic pregnancy with hemodynamic instability; surgical management is the only definitive treatment. Prior PID and prior ipsilateral ectopic pregnancy are significant risk factors for recurrence. None other.

Sex: Male

Complaint: Mild localized low back ache that developed after several hours of gardening, involving bending and lifting bags of soil. Pain is non-radiating, with no numbness, tingling, weakness, or bowel/bladder changes.

Analysis: The presentation is consistent with acute non-specific mechanical low back pain (lumbar strain/sprain) triggered by a clear mechanical event. Supporting findings include localized paraspinal tenderness, mildly reduced flexion, negative straight leg raise bilaterally, and a normal lower-extremity neurological examination. No red flags are present: no neurological deficits, no bowel/bladder dysfunction, no systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss), no significant trauma, and no prior back surgery or chronic back problems. Differential considerations include lumbar muscle strain (most likely), acute lumbosacral disc herniation (less likely given absence of radiculopathy and negative straight leg raise), lumbar spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis, facet joint irritation, and sacroiliac joint dysfunction. Serious causes such as cauda equina syndrome, vertebral fracture, infection, or malignancy are effectively excluded by the clinical picture.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. Imaging (X-ray, MRI) and laboratory testing are not indicated for acute non-specific low back pain without red flags, per current guidelines.

Conclusion: This is a benign, self-limiting acute mechanical lumbar strain. The prognosis is excellent, with expected improvement within days to a few weeks. No urgent or emergent intervention is needed; self-care and conservative management are appropriate.

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate

Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics

- Reassure the patient that this is a common, self-limiting condition with an excellent prognosis.
- Advise staying active and avoiding prolonged bed rest; encourage gradual return to normal activities as tolerated.
- Recommend short-term over-the-counter analgesics (e.g., acetaminophen or NSAIDs) for pain control, if tolerated; note that medication allergies are not specified and should be reviewed before prescribing.

winner_protocol:
Age: 35 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: A 1-week history of an itchy rash in the groin folds that worsens after running and sweating; no genital lesions, urinary symptoms, or prior similar episodes.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for tinea cruris (jock itch), a superficial dermatophyte infection. Strong supporting facts include bilateral, well-demarcated erythematous plaques with slightly raised scaly borders along the inguinal creases extending to the proximal inner thighs, scrotal sparing, and exacerbation by sweating and friction from regular jogging. The absence of satellite lesions and scrotal sparing argue against candidal intertrigo, which often involves the scrotum and shows satellite pustules. Other differential considerations include inverse psoriasis, erythrasma, and contact dermatitis; erythrasma can be distinguished by coral-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp, and inverse psoriasis may require biopsy if uncertain. No red flags are present: the patient is afebrile, has no systemic symptoms, no inguinal lymphadenopathy, and no signs of secondary bacterial infection, ulceration, or necrosis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of skin scrapings to identify fungal hyphae; Wood's lamp examination to differentiate erythrasma; fungal culture if KOH is negative or if atypical features are present.
Conclusion: This is a non-emergent, localized superficial fungal infection of the groin (tinea cruris) in an otherwise healthy patient, without systemic involvement or complications. It is readily manageable on an outpatient basis with topical antifungal therapy and hygiene measures.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Initiate topical antifungal therapy (e.g., terbinafine 1% cream or clotrimazole 1% cream) applied to the affected area and extending slightly beyond the margins, twice daily for 2–4 weeks. Advise keeping the groin area dry, drying thoroughly after bathing, changing out of sweaty clothing immediately after running, and wearing loose-fitting, moisture-wicking cotton underwear. Examine the feet for concurrent tinea pedis (athlete's foot), as autoinoculation from feet to groin is a common route of infection, and treat if present. Avoid topical corticosteroids, which can exacerbate the fungal infection and lead to tinea incognito. Educate the patient on hygiene measures, including not sharing towels or clothing, to prevent recurrence and transmission. winner_protocol:
Age: 22
Sex: Female
Complaint: Left knee injury sustained two days ago during a soccer game while pivoting; sudden pop followed by immediate swelling, inability to bear weight, and continued use of crutches. No prior knee injuries.
Analysis: The mechanism (non-contact pivoting with a pop), immediate effusion, inability to bear weight, positive Lachman test with a soft endpoint, and increased anterior tibial translation on anterior drawer testing are classic findings for an acute anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear. The equivocal McMurray test raises the possibility of a concurrent meniscal injury, which is common in ACL injuries. Collateral ligaments are stable and distal neurovascular status is intact. Differential considerations include meniscal tear, posterior cruciate ligament injury, patellar dislocation/subluxation, osteochondral injury, bone bruise, and tibial plateau or Segond fracture. No red-flag findings (neurovascular compromise, compartment syndrome, open injury, or systemic signs) are present.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Plain radiographs of the left knee (AP, lateral, and sunrise/patellar views) to rule out fracture (e.g., tibial plateau, tibial spine avulsion, Segond fracture); MRI of the left knee to confirm the ACL tear and assess menisci, cartilage, and other ligaments.
Conclusion: Acute anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear of the left knee, with possible associated meniscal injury, in a young active athlete. The patient is stable and neurovascularly intact; the condition requires timely but non-emergent orthopedic evaluation.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Continue protected weight-bearing with crutches; apply RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation); use a hinged knee brace or immobilizer for joint protection; prescribe NSAIDs or analgesics as needed for pain and inflammation; initiate physical therapy for range of motion and quadriceps activation; refer promptly to orthopedics (ideally sports medicine) for definitive evaluation and management. For a high-level athlete, early ACL reconstruction (within 3–6 weeks) with pre-operative rehabilitation is generally recommended to restore stability and allow return to sport; a structured non-operative rehabilitation program may be considered if the patient declines surgery, though it carries a higher risk of instability and future meniscal injury. The final decision depends on MRI findings and patient preferences. Address the possibility of concurrent meniscal injury, which cannot be excluded given the equivocal McMurray test and pain-limited examination; MRI will clarify.
Notes: None

Vignette:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician by his mother who noticed patches of hair loss on his scalp over the past 3 weeks. The patches have been gradually enlarging and the affected areas appear scaly. He attends elementary school and his mother reports several classmates have had similar issues. He denies pain but admits to mild itching. On examination, there are two well-defined round patches of alopecia on the parietal and occipital scalp, measuring approximately 3 cm and 2 cm in diameter respectively. Within the patches, the hair shafts are broken off at the surface giving a black-dot appearance. The surrounding scalp is covered with fine gray-white scale. There is mild posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. A Wood lamp examination reveals no fluorescence. KOH preparation of plucked hairs shows endothrix spores surrounding and within the hair shaft.
winner_protocol:
Age: 6-year-old
Sex: Male
Complaint: Gradually enlarging, well-defined scaly patches of hair loss on the parietal and occipital scalp over the past 3 weeks, with broken hairs giving a black-dot appearance, mild itching, and no pain. Several classmates have had similar issues.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for tinea capitis, an endothrix dermatophyte infection of the scalp. The strongest supporting facts are the well-defined round patches of alopecia with broken hairs at the surface (black-dot appearance), fine gray-white scale, mild posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and KOH preparation showing endothrix spores within and surrounding the hair shaft. The negative Wood lamp fluorescence is consistent with Trichophyton tonsurans, the most common cause of endothrix tinea capitis in the US, which does not fluoresce (unlike Microsporum species, which are ectothrix and fluoresce). The school outbreak context and the patient's age are typical for this infection. Main differential considerations include alopecia areata, seborrheic dermatitis, psoriasis of the scalp, traction alopecia, trichotillomania, and bacterial folliculitis; however, the black-dot hairs and endothrix spores on KOH specifically distinguish tinea capitis from these non-infectious or non-fungal entities. No immediate red flags are present; the child is stable with only mild itching and no systemic symptoms, though untreated infection risks permanent scarring alopecia and kerion formation.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Fungal culture of plucked hairs or scalp scrapings to confirm the species and guide treatment (optional but useful for epidemiology or refractory cases); KOH preparation has already been performed and is positive. Screening of close contacts (family members and classmates) for asymptomatic carriage or infection is indicated.
Conclusion: This is tinea capitis, most likely due to Trichophyton tonsurans, presenting as an endothrix infection with scaly alopecic patches, black-dot hairs, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and positive KOH for endothrix spores. It is a common, treatable, contagious fungal infection in school-aged children that requires prompt but non-emergent outpatient management with systemic antifungal therapy to prevent spread and scarring.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Initiate oral antifungal therapy, as topical agents alone cannot penetrate the hair follicle. Griseofulvin (20–25 mg/kg/day for 6–8 weeks) is the traditional first-line option for T. tonsurans; oral terbinafine is an accepted alternative. Griseofulvin requires intake with fatty food for optimal absorption; consider monitoring CBC/liver function with prolonged courses, and baseline liver function tests for terbinafine. Add adjunctive antifungal shampoo (ketoconazole or selenium sulfide) 2–3 times weekly to reduce shedding and contagion. Educate the family on hygiene: avoid sharing combs, hats, pillows, and towels; wash bedding and personal items. Screen household contacts and treat if infected; prophylactic treatment of close contacts may be considered given the school outbreak. The child may attend school once treatment is initiated but should avoid close contact sports and sharing personal items; note that some school policies may require staying home until 48 hours after initiation of therapy. Schedule follow-up in 2–4 weeks to assess response and monitor for side effects; repeat KOH if no improvement. Check for coexisting tinea corporis on other body sites. If no response to initial therapy, consider alternative antifungals, non-compliance, or culture for susceptibility. Watch for development of a boggy, tender mass (kerion), fever, or signs of secondary bacterial infection (purulent crusting, cellulitis), which would require urgent evaluation, possible oral corticosteroids, surgical drainage, or systemic antibiotics. Assess for immunodeficiency if infections are recurrent or unusually severe.
Notes: The negative Wood lamp fluorescence and endothrix spores on KOH strongly support T. tonsurans, the most common cause in the US. Posterior cervical lymphadenopathy is a common supporting finding. Asymptomatic carrier state in household contacts is common with T. tonsurans, so screen family members. Consider drug interactions (less relevant in a 6-year-old). Resistance patterns of T. tonsurans versus Microsporum canis may influence antifungal choice.

Sex: Male
Complaint: Swollen, tender upper lip after a bee sting at a picnic; the patient was crying hysterically but was calm after 15 minutes.
Analysis: The patient presents with a clear history of a bee sting followed by localized swelling and tenderness of the upper lip. The absence of tongue swelling, drooling, stridor, rash, respiratory distress, hypotension, vomiting, or altered mental status indicates a localized allergic reaction (large local reaction/isolated angioedema) rather than systemic anaphylaxis. Main differential considerations include cellulitis/infection of the lip, traumatic lip injury, hereditary or acquired angioedema, contact dermatitis, and dental abscess extending to the lip; these are distinguished by signs such as fever, erythema, pain out of proportion, history of trauma, or recurrent episodes without an obvious trigger. Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. No urgent laboratory tests or imaging are indicated; a focused physical exam and vital signs are sufficient. Allergy testing may be considered later on an outpatient basis.
Conclusion: This is a localized allergic reaction to a bee sting without systemic involvement or airway compromise. The patient is low-risk but warrants a brief observation period to rule out delayed progression before discharge with strict return precautions.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Observe the child for a few hours and monitor vital signs, with close attention to the airway. Administer an oral antihistamine (e.g., cetirizine or diphenhydramine) and apply a cold compress to the lip; oral analgesics (e.g., acetaminophen or ibuprofen) may be given for pain. A short course of an oral corticosteroid may be considered to reduce swelling. Epinephrine is not indicated currently, as there are no signs of systemic anaphylaxis or imminent airway compromise. Discharge if the swelling is stable or improving, no systemic symptoms develop, and the patient can tolerate oral intake. Provide written education on signs of anaphylaxis to watch for (progressive lip or tongue swelling, stridor, drooling, wheezing, hypotension, generalized urticaria, respiratory distress) with instructions to return immediately if these develop. Arrange outpatient pediatric allergy/immunology evaluation for possible venom allergy testing, education on avoidance, and consideration of venom immunotherapy, as even isolated reactions can herald more severe future responses.

Vignette:
A 32-year-old woman presents with a 10-month history of recurrent episodes of abdominal cramping and altered bowel habits. She describes lower abdominal pain that is relieved with defecation, alternating between periods of diarrhea lasting several days and constipation lasting a week. Symptoms worsen during periods of work-related stress. She denies blood in her stool, nocturnal symptoms, fever, or weight loss. Family history is negative for inflammatory bowel disease or colorectal cancer. On examination, vital signs are normal. She appears anxious but in no acute distress. Abdominal examination reveals mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant with a palpable sigmoid colon on deep palpation. No masses, organomegaly, or guarding. Rectal examination is normal. Complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, C-reactive protein, and thyroid function tests are within normal limits. Stool calprotectin is negative.
winner_protocol:
Age: 32 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: A 32-year-old woman presents with a 10-month history of recurrent episodes of abdominal cramping and altered bowel habits, characterized by lower abdominal pain relieved by defecation and alternating periods of diarrhea lasting several days and constipation lasting a week. Symptoms worsen during periods of work-related stress. She denies blood in stool, nocturnal symptoms, fever, or weight loss, and family history is negative for inflammatory bowel disease or colorectal cancer.
Analysis: The clinical presentation meets Rome IV criteria for Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS), mixed type (IBS-M): recurrent abdominal pain for at least 3 months associated with defecation and changes in stool frequency and form, with alternating diarrhea and constipation, pain relieved by defecation, and stress-related exacerbation. Supporting features include the absence of alarm features (no hematochezia, nocturnal symptoms, fever, or weight loss), negative family history of IBD or colorectal cancer, normal vital signs, no acute distress, and a normal examination except for mild left lower quadrant tenderness with a palpable sigmoid colon (consistent with spasm or stool). Laboratory workup is unremarkable: CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, CRP, and thyroid function tests are within normal limits, and stool calprotectin is negative, effectively ruling out significant organic inflammation. The main differential considerations include inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis), celiac disease, microscopic colitis (especially lymphocytic, which can present with normal calprotectin), thyroid dysfunction, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, chronic intestinal infection (e.g., Giardia), colorectal neoplasia, and medication-induced bowel changes; however, these are largely excluded by the current findings and absence of red flags. The patient's anxious appearance and stress-related symptom exacerbation also warrant consideration of coexisting anxiety or depression as part of the biopsychosocial model of IBS.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None strictly required at this time, as the current workup (CBC, CMP, CRP, thyroid function tests, stool calprotectin) is complete and normal. Optional considerations include celiac serology (tTG-IgA with total IgA) given overlapping symptoms and that it was not explicitly tested, and stool studies (ova/parasite exam) if infectious etiology is suspected based on travel or exposure history. Colonoscopy is not indicated given the absence of alarm features in this age group.
Conclusion: This is a classic presentation of Irritable Bowel Syndrome, mixed type (IBS-M), in a 32-year-old woman. The diagnosis is supported by Rome IV criteria, absence of alarm features, normal laboratory and inflammatory markers, negative stool calprotectin, and a benign physical examination. The condition is chronic but non-progressive and benign, with no organic sequelae. Management should be outpatient, symptom-targeted, and biopsychosocial in approach, with reassurance and longitudinal follow-up.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology
Recommendations: 
1. Provide patient education and reassurance that IBS is a benign functional disorder, explaining the role of diet and stress in symptom flares.
2. Recommend lifestyle and dietary modifications: regular meals, increased soluble fiber, adequate hydration and exercise, and a trial of a low-FODMAP diet; obtain a dietary history to identify triggers (e.g., lactose intolerance, FODMAP sensitivity).
3. Advise stress reduction techniques such as mindfulness or cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), given the stress-related exacerbation and anxious appearance.
4. Screen for anxiety and depression, as these commonly coexist with IBS and may influence symptom severity.
5. Consider symptom-targeted pharmacotherapy: antispasmodics for pain, osmotic laxatives for constipation, loperamide for diarrhea, and low-dose tricyclic antidepressants if pain persists or symptoms are refractory.
6. Review current medications, supplements, and laxative history, as some agents can cause or worsen diarrhea or constipation; document prior treatments tried and their efficacy.
7. Consider optional testing: celiac serology (tTG-IgA with total IgA) given overlapping symptoms; stool studies if infectious etiology is suspected; lactulose breath test for SIBO if clinically indicated.
8. Consider microscopic colitis (especially lymphocytic) if diarrhea-predominant symptoms dominate, and bile acid malabsorption if diarrhea persists and is refractory.
9. Assess pregnancy status and reproductive history in this 32-year-old woman, and consider the potential impact of the menstrual cycle on IBS symptoms.
10. Inquire about recent travel or antibiotic use that could predispose to infectious or post-infectious IBS, and explore family history of functional GI disorders.
11. Arrange routine outpatient follow-up to assess treatment response and monitor for any new alarm features (new bleeding, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, fever); colonoscopy would be warranted only if the patient develops new red flags or reaches the appropriate age threshold (45-50 years).
12. Advise the patient to keep a symptom diary and outline when to seek care for new or worsening symptoms.
Notes: None

Complaint: Sudden onset of severe, constant, throbbing perianal pain (8/10) that began during straining with a bowel movement, worse with sitting and defecation, associated with a palpable lump at the anal verge in a patient with a history of intermittent hemorrhoidal symptoms.
Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for a thrombosed external hemorrhoid. Strongest supporting facts include the acute onset of severe perianal pain after straining, the presence of a tense, bluish-purple, spherical, tender nodule (~2 cm) at the anal verge, and the absence of fever, purulent drainage, or erythema suggesting infection. Predisposing risk factors include prolonged sitting (10–12 hours daily as a truck driver), a low-fiber diet, poor fluid intake, and prior hemorrhoidal disease. The diagnosis is clinical. Main differential considerations include perianal abscess, anal fissure, prolapsed/strangulated internal hemorrhoid, perianal hematoma, and less likely anorectal malignancy or necrotizing soft tissue infection (e.g., Fournier's gangrene), which would be suggested by red flags such as fever, spreading erythema, systemic toxicity, or disproportionate pain.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. The diagnosis is clinical; no laboratory or imaging studies are routinely indicated. Digital rectal exam was appropriately deferred due to pain and may be performed once pain subsides. Anoscopy may be considered after pain is controlled if internal pathology is suspected.
Conclusion: This is a thrombosed external hemorrhoid in a patient with significant occupational and dietary risk factors. The condition is painful but not life-threatening; it requires prompt non-emergent outpatient evaluation and management, with surgical excision a valid option given presentation within 72 hours of onset.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery
Recommendations: Manage as urgent outpatient care, ideally within 48–72 hours of onset. Offer conservative measures (sitz baths, stool softeners, fiber supplementation, adequate hydration, topical anesthetics, and analgesics such as NSAIDs) or surgical excision/incision and clot removal, particularly given symptom onset was yesterday and pain is severe. Before any surgical intervention, assess for anticoagulant/antiplatelet use and bleeding disorders (coagulopathy). Assess for immunocompromise (diabetes, HIV, immunosuppressive medications), which increases infection risk. Counsel on lifestyle modifications to prevent recurrence: high-fiber diet (25–30 g/day), adequate hydration, avoidance of straining, regular bowel habits, and use of stool softeners. Address occupational factors: advise scheduled breaks, mobility, and ergonomic adjustments for prolonged sitting. Consider colorectal cancer screening given age 55 and history of bleeding, as the patient may be overdue for colonoscopy. Schedule follow-up in 1–2 weeks, and perform a deferred digital rectal exam once pain subsides to evaluate for internal hemorrhoids or other pathology. Advise the patient to return urgently if red flags develop (fever, chills, purulent drainage, spreading erythema, severe rectal bleeding, urinary retention, rapid enlargement of the mass, or signs of systemic toxicity).
Notes: Exclude Fournier's gangrene (necrotizing fasciitis) as a rare but life-threatening differential, especially if pain is disproportionate or rapidly progressive. Maintain perianal hygiene to reduce risk of skin infection from moisture due to prolonged sitting. Consider previous anorectal surgery or coexisting anal fissures. Chronic hemorrhoidal disease indicates need for long-term management and prevention of recurrence.

Age: 22
Sex: Male
Complaint: A 22-year-old student presents with a 5-year history of worsening nasal congestion, sneezing, and nasal itching. Symptoms are year-round but worse in spring, accompanied by eye itching, redness, tearing, and palate and throat itching during the spring season. The patient has a history of infantile eczema.

Analysis: The clinical picture is most consistent with allergic rhinitis (perennial with seasonal exacerbation) associated with allergic conjunctivitis, occurring in the context of an atopic diathesis. Strong supporting facts include the chronic nasal symptoms (congestion, sneezing, itching), the clear seasonal worsening in spring, the classic ocular (itching, redness, tearing) and oropharyngeal (palate and throat itching) symptoms, and the personal history of infantile eczema, which indicates an atopic predisposition. The year-round nature with spring exacerbation suggests sensitization to both perennial and seasonal allergens. Main differential considerations include non-allergic (vasomotor) rhinitis, chronic rhinosinusitis, nasal polyposis, infectious rhinitis, rhinitis medicamentosa (from decongestant overuse), and structural abnormalities such as a deviated septum. These should be excluded based on history, physical examination, and investigations, especially if symptoms are atypical or unresponsive to initial therapy. No red flags (unilateral symptoms, epistaxis, facial pain, vision changes, systemic signs) are present in the vignette, supporting a benign, non-emergent allergic process.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Skin prick testing or serum-specific IgE testing for relevant aeroallergens (pollens, dust mites, mold, animal dander); nasal endoscopy to evaluate for polyps or structural issues; spirometry to screen for coexisting asthma; CBC with differential to assess eosinophilia; ocular examination if conjunctivitis is prominent.

Conclusion: This is a case of allergic rhinitis (perennial with seasonal exacerbation) with associated allergic conjunctivitis in a young atopic patient. The condition is chronic and bothersome but not life-threatening, with no acute distress, respiratory compromise, or signs of anaphylaxis. It warrants routine outpatient evaluation and management, with a focus on allergen avoidance, pharmacologic therapy, and screening for atopic comorbidities.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)

Recommendations:
1. Initiate intranasal corticosteroids (e.g., fluticasone) as first-line therapy for nasal symptoms.
2. Add oral or intranasal second-generation antihistamines (e.g., cetirizine) for sneezing and itching.
3. Use topical ocular antihistamines or mast cell stabilizers for conjunctival symptoms.
4. Recommend allergen avoidance: staying indoors during high pollen counts, using air filters, and addressing indoor allergens (dust mites, pets, mold) and tobacco smoke exposure.
5. Consider saline nasal irrigation as a supportive measure.
6. If symptoms are severe or refractory, consider leukotriene receptor antagonists or allergen immunotherapy (candidacy should be assessed).
7. Screen for asthma and other atopic comorbidities (eczema, allergic rhinitis) given the atopic march; assess impact on sleep, daytime somnolence, and academic/work performance.
8. Document family history of atopy and review medication history to exclude rhinitis medicamentosa from decongestant overuse.
9. Check for physical signs: allergic shiners, nasal crease, mouth breathing.
10. Monitor for complications: nasal polyps, chronic sinusitis, sleep-disordered breathing.
11. Educate the patient on proper use of nasal sprays and eye drops, the chronic nature of the condition, and when to seek urgent care (e.g., severe breathing difficulty, vision changes).
12. Schedule follow-up in 4-6 weeks to assess response and adjust therapy; refer to ENT and/or Allergy-Immunology if symptoms persist despite optimized therapy or if there is suspicion of nasal polyps or asthma.

Notes: Unilateral symptoms, persistent epistaxis, or asymmetric findings warrant evaluation for structural or neoplastic causes. Monitor for side effects of intranasal steroids (epistaxis, crusting) and ensure proper administration technique. No red flags are present in the current case, but they should be actively ruled out during evaluation.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old woman presents in January with 2-day history of fever, cough, headache, and generalized weakness. She was in her usual state of health before an abrupt onset of these symptoms. A few viral illnesses have affected her during the current winter, but not to this severity. She reports sick contacts at work and did not receive the seasonal influenza vaccine this season.

Age: 30
Sex: Female
Complaint: Two-day history of abrupt-onset fever, cough, headache, and generalized weakness presenting in January, with reported sick contacts at work and no seasonal influenza vaccination this season.

Analysis: The clinical presentation is most consistent with an uncomplicated influenza-like illness. Supporting features include the abrupt onset of fever, cough, headache, and generalized weakness during peak influenza season (January), reported sick contacts, and lack of seasonal influenza vaccination. The patient was previously in her usual state of health, and no red-flag symptoms (dyspnea, chest pain, confusion, hemodynamic instability, neck stiffness, or signs of dehydration) are reported. The main differential considerations include influenza, COVID-19, other viral upper respiratory infections (e.g., RSV, rhinovirus, adenovirus), and early bacterial or atypical pneumonia. Meningitis is a less likely consideration given the headache but should be kept in mind if headache is severe with neck stiffness or photophobia. The patient is a young adult without stated comorbidities, suggesting lower overall risk, but assessment for hidden risk factors (pregnancy, underlying chronic conditions, immunosuppression) is warranted. The case does not indicate the need for emergency department care; timely non-emergent evaluation is appropriate, ideally within 48 hours of symptom onset to allow antiviral consideration.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Rapid influenza diagnostic test or influenza PCR; SARS-CoV-2 testing; complete blood count if bacterial superinfection is suspected; chest radiograph only if respiratory distress, focal lung findings, or other red flags develop. Routine labs are not necessarily required in the absence of complications.

Conclusion: This is an uncomplicated influenza-like illness in a previously healthy 30-year-old woman, most likely seasonal influenza, requiring non-emergent evaluation and management in a primary care or general medicine setting. The patient is stable with no red-flag features, and management should focus on supportive care, consideration of antiviral therapy if within 48 hours of symptom onset, testing for influenza and COVID-19, and monitoring for complications such as secondary bacterial pneumonia.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

Subclinical specialization: General Medicine

Recommendations: Evaluate the patient in a timely manner, ideally within 48 hours of symptom onset, to allow consideration of antiviral therapy (e.g., oseltamivir) if indicated. Perform rapid influenza testing and SARS-CoV-2 testing to confirm etiology and guide management and infection control. Provide supportive care with antipyretics (e.g., acetaminophen), adequate hydration, and rest. Assess pregnancy status, as pregnancy is a high-risk condition for influenza complications and affects antiviral decisions. Evaluate for underlying comorbidities (asthma, diabetes, immunosuppression, chronic heart or lung disease) that increase risk of complications. Advise the patient on red-flag warning signs (dyspnea, chest pain, confusion, persistent high fever beyond 3–5 days, hemoptysis, inability to tolerate oral intake, signs of dehydration, severe headache with neck stiffness or photophobia) and instruct her to seek urgent care if these develop. Recommend isolation and infection control measures (hand hygiene, masking) to prevent transmission, and consider public health reporting if a workplace outbreak is suspected. Review vaccination history beyond influenza (COVID-19, pneumococcal) to inform differential and prevention. Schedule re-evaluation in 48–72 hours or sooner if symptoms worsen, and recommend seasonal influenza vaccination in the future. Monitor for secondary bacterial pneumonia (e.g., pneumococcal, staphylococcal) if symptoms worsen or fever recurs, and be aware of rare complications such as myocarditis/pericarditis if chest pain or palpitations develop. Review the medication list for potential interactions with antivirals (e.g., probenecid) and consider socio-economic factors that may affect access to testing or medication.

Notes: None

winner_protocol:
Age: 38
Sex: Male
Complaint: Perianal discomfort and a small palpable lump noticed 3 days ago, with mild itching after prolonged sitting; no bleeding, pain with defecation, fever, or change in bowel habits.
Analysis: The lesion is a small (≈5 mm), soft, non-tender, external perianal skin tag at the 6 o'clock position, without thrombosis, bleeding, prolapse, or surrounding erythema. These features are classic for a benign external skin tag (acrochordon/fibroepithelial polyp), likely acquired secondary to chronic perianal venous congestion from prolonged sitting (8–10 hours daily). The absence of red flags—rectal bleeding, pain, fever, bowel habit changes, and a negative family history of colorectal cancer—supports a benign, non-urgent process. Main differential considerations include thrombosed external hemorrhoid, condyloma acuminatum (HPV), hypertrophied anal papilla, perianal abscess/fistula, anal polyp, sebaceous cyst, and Crohn-related perianal disease; however, the lack of pain, friability, ulceration, or systemic signs makes these less likely. No diagnostic investigations are required at this time; the diagnosis is clinical.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (clinical examination is sufficient; no laboratory tests, imaging, or biopsy indicated unless red flags develop).
Conclusion: This is a benign external perianal skin tag in a sedentary patient, with no features suggesting thrombosis, infection, or malignancy. It is appropriate for conservative, self-care management with routine follow-up if symptoms change.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery
Recommendations: Reassure the patient that the lesion is benign and does not require urgent intervention. Advise modification of sitting habits, including regular breaks and use of a cushion to reduce perianal pressure. Maintain perianal hygiene and consider sitz baths or a topical barrier cream (or short course of mild topical steroid) for itching. Offer surgical excision (e.g., snip-plasty or electrocautery) via General/Colorectal Surgery only if the tag becomes symptomatic (pain, thrombosis, enlargement, functional impairment) or if the patient desires removal for cosmetic reasons. Observe for changes over 4–6 weeks. Address additional considerations: if the lesion grows, becomes friable, multiplies, or risk factors for HPV are present, evaluate for condyloma acuminatum; if itching persists, consider contact dermatitis or fungal infection; if rectal bleeding or bowel habit changes develop, pursue anoscopy or colonoscopy to exclude internal hemorrhoids, fissures, or malignancy; assess dietary fiber and fluid intake to avoid constipation and straining; consider a sexual history if HPV is suspected; and discuss routine colorectal cancer screening despite the negative family history.
Notes: None

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.

Vignette:
A 58-year-old man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh class C) presents after two episodes of large-volume hematemesis over the past hour, each estimated at 500 mL of bright red blood with clots. He also reports black tarry stools for the past 2 days. He has known esophageal varices documented on prior endoscopy and has been non-compliant with propranolol therapy. On examination, he is pale, confused, and in moderate distress. Vital signs: T 36.2C, HR 128, RR 24, BP 78/42, SpO2 94%. Abdominal exam reveals ascites, splenomegaly, and caput medusae. Rectal exam shows melena. Labs: hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL (baseline 10.4), platelets 62,000/mcL, INR 2.4, BUN 58 mg/dL. Two large-bore IVs are placed and massive transfusion protocol is activated.
winner_protocol:
Age: 58
Sex: Male
Complaint: Two episodes of large-volume hematemesis (each ~500 mL of bright red blood with clots) over the past hour, plus black tarry stools for 2 days, in a man with known esophageal varices and alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C) who has been non-compliant with propranolol.

Analysis: The patient presents with acute upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage in the setting of decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis and documented portal hypertension (ascites, splenomegaly, caput medusae, known esophageal varices). The large-volume hematemesis with clots, melena, and hemodynamic instability (BP 78/42, HR 128, confusion, pallor) indicate hemorrhagic shock from active bleeding. Given the known varices and portal hypertensive stigmata, acute esophageal variceal rupture is the most likely source; non-compliance with propranolol (secondary prophylaxis) likely contributed to the event. Differential considerations include gastric varices, portal hypertensive gastropathy, peptic ulcer disease, Mallory-Weiss tear, erosive gastritis, Dieulafoy lesion, and less likely neoplastic lesions; endoscopy is required to confirm the source. Poor prognostic factors present include hemodynamic shock, altered mental status, Child-Pugh C decompensation, active massive bleeding, coagulopathy (INR 2.4), severe thrombocytopenia (62,000/mcL), and severe anemia (Hb 6.2 g/dL).

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Urgent upper endoscopy (EGD) with band ligation capability; type and crossmatch; repeat CBC; coagulation profile; liver function tests; lactate; blood type and screen; arterial blood gas; bedside abdominal ultrasound (FAST) for free fluid; consider CT imaging if endoscopy is not immediately available.

Conclusion: Acute esophageal variceal hemorrhage secondary to portal hypertension from decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C), presenting with hemorrhagic shock and active ongoing bleeding. This is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate resuscitation, vasoactive therapy, antibiotic prophylaxis, and urgent endoscopic hemostasis.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology

Recommendations: Continue the massive transfusion protocol with balanced blood product resuscitation (PRBC:FFP:platelets near 1:1:1), targeting hemoglobin ~7–8 g/dL in cirrhosis. Secure the airway given confusion and active hematemesis to prevent aspiration. Start IV vasoactive therapy (octreotide or terlipressin) immediately and continue for 2–5 days. Administer prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone). Give IV proton pump inhibitor infusion and vitamin K; consider albumin infusion. Arrange urgent therapeutic upper endoscopy with variceal band ligation (or sclerotherapy) once hemodynamically stabilized. Have balloon tamponade (Sengstaken-Blakemore tube) and TIPS available as rescue therapies for refractory bleeding; consider early TIPS if endoscopic control fails. After stabilization, initiate secondary prophylaxis with a non-selective beta-blocker, manage ascites (diuretics, paracentesis), and monitor renal function.

Notes: The patient's non-compliance with propranolol likely contributed to the bleeding episode. Child-Pugh C cirrhosis with active variceal bleeding carries very high short-term mortality; restrictive transfusion strategy in cirrhosis reduces rebleeding and mortality. Airway protection is critical given altered mental status and active vomiting.

yr-old man who possibly had a stroke. At the store, they found him lying on the ground
unconscious but breathing normally. After their arrival, the patient awoke but was unable to give
coherent responses to questions or commands.
Store employees who saw the patient reported to EMTs that he fell to the ground suddenly from
a sitting position, then began drooling, and his arms and legs shook for what seemed to be a
long time, but they cannot quantify how long. They state he had not appeared ill before the
event.

Not available at this time.

General apperance: Awake; saliva and blood at corner of his mouth. He appears well-

Age: 50 years  
Sex: Male  

Complaint:  
Sudden loss of consciousness with witnessed tonic‑clonic activity, postictal confusion, transient severe bradycardia and hypotension, and a subtle residual left‑upper‑extremity dysdiadochokinesia.

Analysis:  
The clinical presentation is most consistent with a first generalized tonic‑clonic seizure followed by a postictal state. Supporting features include the sudden fall from a sitting position, drooling, bilateral limb shaking, tongue puncture wound (indicating tongue biting), urinary incontinence, and the gradual recovery to alertness with residual confusion. The transient episode of bradycardia (HR 30) and hypotension (BP 74/52) with respiratory depression likely reflects postictal autonomic dysfunction or possibly increased intracranial pressure; the ECG showed sinus rhythm without arrhythmia, and the patient spontaneously recovered to normal sinus rhythm, making a primary cardiac cause less likely.  

The focal finding of left‑upper‑extremity dysdiadochokinesia localizes to the right hemisphere (parietal or cerebellar connections). This new deficit, along with the first‑time seizure in an adult over 50, mandates urgent neuroimaging. The head CT interpretation is debated among the experts: some favor intraparenchymal hemorrhage, others an early ischemic stroke, and others mild cerebral edema. The CT findings are not definitive, and the differential includes acute ischemic stroke with symptomatic seizure, intraparenchymal hemorrhage, subarachnoid hemorrhage, brain tumor, CNS infection, metabolic derangement, and toxic ingestion. The absence of fever, leukocytosis, and normal serum chemistry reduces the likelihood of infection or metabolic causes. The patient’s baseline hypertension and use of aspirin and fish oil are relevant to bleeding risk and stroke mechanism.  

Given the transient life‑threatening hemodynamic instability and the new focal deficit, this is an emergent neurological condition requiring immediate comprehensive evaluation and monitoring.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests:  
- MRI brain with diffusion‑weighted imaging (DWI) to confirm or exclude acute ischemic stroke and to better characterize any structural lesion.  
- Electroencephalogram (EEG) to evaluate for ongoing seizure activity or epileptiform discharges.  
- Continuous cardiac telemetry and serial troponin measurements to assess for arrhythmia or myocardial injury.  
- Laboratory workup: complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation profile, toxicology screen, and blood glucose.  
- Carotid duplex ultrasound and echocardiography (transthoracic or transesophageal) as part of the stroke workup to identify embolic sources.  
- Neurosurgery consultation if imaging reveals hemorrhage, mass effect, or hydrocephalus.

Conclusion:  
The patient experienced a first generalized tonic‑clonic seizure with a postictal state, complicated by transient autonomic instability (bradycardia and hypotension). A subtle left‑upper‑extremity dysdiadochokinesia suggests a right‑hemisphere structural lesion. The head CT is not definitive, and the differential includes acute ischemic stroke, intraparenchymal hemorrhage, or early cerebral edema. This is a neurological emergency requiring emergent care, admission, and further diagnostic evaluation.

Emergency type:  
Requires emergent care  

Subclinical specialization:  
Neurology  

Recommendations:  
- Admit the patient to an intensive care unit or a monitored neurology/stroke unit for continuous cardiac and neurologic monitoring.  
- Initiate neurology consultation immediately; involve neurosurgery if hemorrhage or mass effect is identified.  
- Maintain airway protection and monitor respiratory status, especially given the transient respiratory depression and tongue injury.  
- If seizure activity recurs, administer a benzodiazepine (e.g., lorazepam) and consider a loading dose of an antiepileptic (e.g., levetiracetam) for secondary prevention.  
- Manage blood pressure carefully: the initial hypertension (165/90) should be lowered modestly to reduce the risk of hemorrhagic conversion, but avoid aggressive reduction if ischemic stroke is suspected.  
- Address the punctate red spots on the right lower leg: evaluate for petechiae, which may indicate a bleeding disorder, vasculitis, or post‑ictal rash; consider coagulation studies and dermatologic assessment.  
- The tongue puncture wound raises concern for aspiration; ensure oral hygiene and monitor for infection.  
- Review the patient’s medications: aspirin and fish oil may affect platelet function and bleeding risk; discuss with neurology before initiating antithrombotic therapy.  
- The transient bradycardia/hypotension could be postictal autonomic dysfunction or ictal bradycardia; consider cardiac monitoring and evaluation for SUDEP risk.  
- The persistence of dysdiadochokinesia after full alertness suggests a structural lesion rather than Todd’s paralysis; MRI is essential to confirm the diagnosis.  
- Given the patient’s occupation as an attorney, discuss driving restrictions and occupational safety implications after a first seizure.  
- Provide education to the patient and family about seizure precautions, medication adherence, and the need for follow‑up with neurology.

Notes:  
- The head CT interpretation is not definitive; the experts diverged among intraparenchymal hemorrhage, ischemic stroke, and mild cerebral edema. MRI with DWI is required to clarify the diagnosis.  
- The patient’s history of well‑controlled asthma should be considered if sedatives or benzodiazepines are administered.  
- The absence of fever, leukocytosis, and normal serum chemistry makes CNS infection or metabolic derangement less likely, but these should still be excluded with appropriate testing.  
- The transient bradycardia and hypotension resolved spontaneously; however, close monitoring is warranted to detect recurrence or signs of increased intracranial pressure.  
- The punctate red spots on the right lower leg and the tongue puncture wound are important physical findings that support the seizure diagnosis and warrant further evaluation.

winner_protocol:
Age: 16 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Progressive right ear pain and itching of 4 days' duration, with a sensation of fullness and mild hearing reduction. Pain is exacerbated by chewing and by lying on the right side. The patient has been swimming daily for 3 weeks during summer training.
Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for acute otitis externa (swimmer's ear). The strongest supporting facts are the recent frequent water exposure, the marked tenderness on tragus manipulation and auricular traction, and the otoscopic findings of a narrowed, edematous external auditory canal with erythematous, macerated skin and scant white debris, with an intact tympanic membrane. The absence of fever, ear discharge, periauricular lymphadenopathy, mastoid tenderness, and facial nerve dysfunction indicates an uncomplicated, localized infection without extension beyond the external canal. Main differential considerations include acute otitis media (less likely given the intact tympanic membrane, canal inflammation, and manipulation tenderness), furunculosis, contact/allergic dermatitis of the canal, fungal otitis externa, and malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa (excluded by the absence of red flags and the patient's otherwise healthy status). The diagnosis is clinical, and no routine diagnostic testing is indicated.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. A thorough otoscopic examination is sufficient for diagnosis. Cultures of the ear canal are not routinely indicated unless the condition is refractory to initial treatment or atypical organisms are suspected; imaging is not needed given the absence of red flags.
Conclusion: This is an uncomplicated acute otitis externa (swimmer's ear) in an otherwise healthy adolescent. The infection is localized to the external auditory canal with no evidence of systemic involvement or complications. Prompt outpatient management is appropriate.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Initiate topical antimicrobial ear drops (e.g., a fluoroquinolone such as ciprofloxacin, often combined with a corticosteroid like dexamethasone) administered twice daily, or an antiseptic preparation (e.g., acetic acid) as an alternative. Prescribe analgesics (NSAIDs or acetaminophen) for pain control. Instruct the patient to keep the ear dry and avoid swimming and water entry into the ear until resolution. Advise against the use of cotton swabs in the ear canal. Re-evaluate in 48–72 hours; if there is no improvement, or if pain worsens, fever develops, spreading erythema, otorrhea, or progressive hearing loss occurs, consider oral antibiotics, possible systemic steroids, or imaging (CT), and refer to ENT urgently. Primary care can initiate treatment, but ENT referral is appropriate for confirmation, possible aural toilet, and follow-up if needed.
Notes: The tympanic membrane was barely visible but appeared intact; if the canal edema is severe enough to preclude adequate delivery of topical drops, placement of an ear wick may be necessary. Red flags that would change management include fever, purulent otorrhea, periauricular lymphadenopathy, mastoid tenderness, facial nerve dysfunction, or inability to visualize the tympanic membrane due to severe canal stenosis, all of which are absent in this case.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.

Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.

- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
